\title{Transistor-Level Energy Analysis of Signal Processing Algorithms: Beyond Operation Counting}

\begin{document}
\ninept
\maketitle

\begin{abstract}
Energy estimates for signal processing algorithms usually rest on floating-point operation counts, which ignore memory traffic, command overhead, and the gap between textbook formulas and library implementations. We present an energy model based on Transistor Operations (TOs), the physics-grounded cost unit of the TOML framework, and validate it on 37 signal processing algorithms in 8 categories on two NVIDIA GPUs (RTX 4090 and A100 SXM4). Its four fitted coefficients (compute, memory, GPU-command dispatch, fused-sequential step) take measured inputs: analytical operation counts checked against Nsight Compute instruction counts, and per-invocation GPU command counts measured with Nsight Systems. It predicts energy with median errors of \mdapea\% and \mdapeb\%, places \withinTwoa\% and \withinTwob\% of configurations within a factor of two, and ranks \hhPooledPct\% of head-to-head algorithm pairs correctly (\hhPooledLOAOPct\% under leave-one-algorithm-out cross-validation). Profiling confirms the split-radix FFT and 4-FMA complex MAC corrections and shows that library kernels on tiny matrices execute 30 to 500 times the arithmetic count as fixed work per launch. The per-command cost is set by the host (\alphaOa\ vs.\ \alphaOb\,$\mu$J), which sets the payoff of kernel fusion; sequential algorithms are 10 to 100$\times$ more energy-efficient on CPU; and measured energy per operation spans 60$\times$ across floating-point kernels, which bounds any constant-cost-per-operation model.
\end{abstract}

\begin{keywords}
Energy efficiency, signal processing, GPU, transistor operations, power measurement
\end{keywords}

% =========================================================================
\section{Introduction}
\label{sec:intro}
% =========================================================================

Energy consumption is a first-order design constraint for signal processing systems, from battery-powered edge devices to datacenter inference pipelines. Practitioners routinely estimate computational cost by counting floating-point operations (FLOPs), yet this metric systematically misrepresents energy. It ignores three physical realities: (i)~memory accesses cost 5 to 200$\times$ more energy than arithmetic~\cite{Horowitz2014}, (ii)~every command issued to a GPU carries a fixed cost that dominates when kernels are small, and (iii)~hardware implementations diverge from textbook operation counts. As a concrete example of~(iii), fused multiply-add units halve complex MAC costs, and cuFFT executes 30\% fewer instructions than the Cooley-Tukey formula predicts.

Prior work on energy-aware computing has focused on neural network accelerators~\cite{Yang2017, Desoli2017}, coarse GPU-level power modeling~\cite{Bridges2016}, node-level power measurement of GPU servers under AI training~\cite{Latif2025, Latif2026}, and validation of software energy estimators against external meters~\cite{Fischer2025}. The Transistor Operations (TO) framework~\cite{Syed2026TOML} introduced physics-grounded energy units anchored to CMOS transistor switching costs at a 45\,nm reference node, achieving $r^2 = 0.961$ across seven deep learning architectures. A subsequent study extended the framework to containerized cloud workloads~\cite{Syed2026TOMLCloud}. Neither study addressed signal processing, where computational patterns differ substantially from neural network inference: FFT butterfly structures, recursive filters, iterative decompositions, and purely comparison-based workloads such as median filtering (which executes zero floating-point instructions on GPU hardware).

This paper makes four contributions:
\begin{enumerate}
\itemsep0pt
\item A four-parameter energy model whose inputs are measured, not assumed: analytical operation counts validated by Nsight Compute for all 37 algorithms, and per-invocation GPU command counts measured by Nsight Systems for every benchmark configuration. On 264 measurements the model has a median error of \mdapea\% and \mdapeb\% on the two GPUs, \withinTwoa\% and \withinTwob\% of predictions within 2$\times$, and \hhPooledPct\% head-to-head ranking accuracy, with leave-one-algorithm-out results reported alongside.
\item Instruction-count validation of two corrections to standard operation counting (split-radix FFT across a size sweep, complex MAC as 4 FMAs), and the finding that library kernels on tiny matrices execute 30 to 500$\times$ the arithmetic count as fixed work per launch, which is what the dispatch term prices.
\item Three sequential energy regimes with a per-command cost that is a property of the host: \alphaOa\,$\mu$J on a laptop and \alphaOb\,$\mu$J on a server, so the payoff of fusing a Python loop into one kernel is \fusionGainMina\ to \fusionGainMaxa$\times$ per timestep on the former and \fusionGainMinb\ to \fusionGainMaxb$\times$ on the latter.
\item A systematic CPU vs.\ GPU energy comparison across all 37 algorithms showing that sequential algorithms are 10 to 100$\times$ more efficient on CPU, with clear category-level crossover guidance.
\end{enumerate}

% =========================================================================
\section{TOML Framework}
\label{sec:framework}
% =========================================================================

\subsection{Transistor Operations}

A Transistor Operation (TO) is a unit of computational cost anchored to CMOS circuit-level energy measurements at a 45\,nm reference node~\cite{Horowitz2014}. At 45\,nm and 0.9\,V, Horowitz reports that a 32-bit floating-point multiply costs 3.7\,pJ and a 32-bit floating-point add costs 0.9\,pJ, giving a multiply-accumulate (MAC) cost of approximately 4.6\,pJ~\cite{Sze2017}. We define 1\,TO $\approx$ 1\,fJ, so that one FP32 MAC corresponds to 5{,}000\,TOs.

\begin{table}[!t]
\centering
\caption{TO cost table at 45\,nm reference node~\cite{Horowitz2014}.}
\label{tab:to_costs}
\begin{tabular}{llr}
\toprule
Category & Operation & TOs \\
\midrule
Arithmetic & MAC (FP32 FMA) & 5{,}000 \\
 & Division / Square root & 15{,}000 \\
 & Exp / Sin / Cos & 18{,}000 \\
 & Tanh & 15{,}000 \\
 & Comparison & 50 \\
\midrule
Activation & ReLU & 100 \\
 & GELU & 20{,}000 \\
 & Softmax (per element) & 25{,}000 \\
\midrule
Memory & SRAM (32-bit word) & 192 \\
 & HBM (32-bit word) & 10{,}000 \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

Table~\ref{tab:to_costs} lists the TO costs used in this work, identical to those in prior studies~\cite{Syed2026TOML, Syed2026TOMLCloud}. Each floating-point operation on a modern GPU dispatches a full fused multiply-add (FMA) unit whether the instruction is an add, multiply, or FMA~\cite{NsightCompute}, so all three map to a single MAC cost. Transcendental functions are evaluated by polynomial approximation or Newton-Raphson iteration, requiring 3 to 4 FMA cycles and hence proportionally higher TO costs. Memory costs are weighted separately: 192\,TOs per 32-bit SRAM word and 10{,}000\,TOs per HBM word, reflecting the hierarchy measured by Horowitz (5\,pJ for 8\,KB SRAM, 640\,pJ for DRAM). These TO values are \emph{relative weights}, not direct energy predictions; the fitted coefficients (Section~\ref{sec:framework_model}) absorb architecture-specific and process-node scaling.

\subsection{Four-Parameter Energy Model}
\label{sec:framework_model}

For each algorithm we derive the compute TO count $T_c$ and memory TO count $T_m$ analytically from the algorithm's mathematical definition, so these counts are architecture-independent. The predicted energy of one GPU invocation is
\begin{equation}
E = \alpha_c \cdot T_c + \alpha_m \cdot T_m + \alpha_o \cdot S_o + \alpha_f \cdot S_f
\label{eq:four_param}
\end{equation}
where $S_o$ is the number of GPU commands (kernel launches, memory copies, and memsets) issued by the invocation, $S_f$ is the number of fused-sequential timesteps, and $\alpha_c, \alpha_m, \alpha_o, \alpha_f \geq 0$ are fitted by non-negative least squares (NNLS). Non-negativity is physical: energy cannot decrease with more computation, memory access, or commands.

\textbf{Compute energy} ($\alpha_c \cdot T_c$). The counts $T_c$ follow from each algorithm's mathematical structure. For FFT we use the split-radix count $4N \log_2 N - 6N + 8$~\cite{Duhamel1990} rather than the Cooley-Tukey count; for complex-valued algorithms we count 4~FMAs per complex MAC instead of 8 real operations. Both choices are checked against instruction counts in Section~\ref{sec:ncu}. $\alpha_c$ absorbs the ratio between operations counted and energy actually spent per operation on each GPU.

\textbf{Memory energy} ($\alpha_m \cdot T_m$). We count HBM words read and written per invocation from each algorithm's data access pattern (inputs, outputs, and intermediate buffers that spill to global memory); on-chip reuse within a kernel counts as SRAM. $\alpha_m$ exceeds $\alpha_c$ on both GPUs, reflecting the energy dominance of data movement.

\textbf{Command dispatch} ($\alpha_o \cdot S_o$). Every command issued to the GPU costs a fixed amount of energy: idle power spent while the host prepares and issues the next command, plus any fixed padded work the kernel executes regardless of its problem size. $S_o$ is measured, not derived: for every benchmark configuration we count the commands of one invocation with Nsight Systems (Section~\ref{sec:census}). Python-loop algorithms (adaptive filters, state estimators, iterative decompositions) issue 7 to 54 commands per iteration and 1{,}300 to 8{,}600 per invocation (the pure-PyTorch IIR fallback used on the A100 issues 22 per sample); library factorizations issue hundreds per call (cuSOLVER SVD 137 to 245, PCA 166); the subspace methods and the Transformer denoiser 16 to 44; batched transforms and filters 1 to 14. The same coefficient prices every command whatever issued it.

\textbf{Fused-sequential} ($\alpha_f \cdot S_f$). Algorithms that process timesteps serially inside a single kernel (cuDNN LSTM at batch size $B = 1$, which launches 6 to 8 kernels for any $N$) issue almost no commands but pay per-timestep energy for serial execution at low GPU utilization.

\section{Experimental Setup}
\label{sec:setup}
% =========================================================================

\label{tab:algorithms}
\begin{tabular}{lrl}
\toprule
Category & \# & Representative algorithms \\
\midrule
Transforms & 8 & FFT, DCT, DST, DWT, STFT, Hilbert \\
Filters & 8 & FIR, IIR, median, Wiener, filterbank \\
Adaptive & 4 & LMS, NLMS, RLS, APA \\
Estimation & 4 & Kalman, EKF, UKF, particle \\
Spectral & 4 & periodogram, Welch, MUSIC, ESPRIT \\
Decomposition & 4 & SVD, PCA, FastICA, NMF \\
Compression & 2 & JPEG (DCT), MDCT audio codec \\
ML-enhanced & 3 & CNN, LSTM, Transformer denoisers \\
\bottomrule
\end{tabular}
\end{table}

\subsection{Algorithm Selection}

We benchmark 37 signal processing algorithms across 8 categories (Table~\ref{tab:algorithms}), spanning embarrassingly parallel transforms, inherently sequential recursive filters, and iterative estimation. All implementations use canonical libraries (PyTorch, SciPy, scikit-learn, PyWavelets, torchaudio)~\cite{PyTorch} rather than custom CUDA kernels, i.e.\ the implementations practitioners actually deploy.

Each algorithm is benchmarked at four signal lengths ($N = 256$, $1024$, $4096$, $16384$) in FP32 precision. GPU batch sizes are $B = 2048$ where parallelizable (transforms, filters, spectral, ML), with smaller $B$ for algorithms whose memory footprint scales with $B \times N$ (e.g., $B = 512$ for direct DFT, $B = 2$ for ESPRIT at $N = 1024$). CPU benchmarks use $B = 1$.

\subsection{Hardware and Power Measurement}

\textbf{GPUs.} An RTX 4090 hosted by an Intel Core i9-14900HX laptop and an A100 SXM4 in a server; GPU power is sampled via NVML at about 20\,Hz. The RTX 4090 yields \nptsa\ benchmark points and the A100 \nptsb.

\textbf{CPU.} The i9-14900HX (8 Performance + 16 Efficiency cores, 55\,W base TDP) is measured via RAPL ``CPU Package'' counters exposed through LibreHardwareMonitor at approximately 217\,Hz, yielding 147 benchmark points.

\textbf{Thermal settling and idle baseline.} Before each measurement we wait for the processor temperature to stabilize within $\pm 1^\circ$C over 5\,s (leakage current is exponential in temperature), then measure idle power per algorithm (3\,s for GPU, 10\,s for CPU), giving $\Delta P = P_{\text{active}} - P_{\text{idle}}$; per-algorithm baselines are needed because idle power drifts with temperature over a multi-hour suite.

\textbf{Measurement loop.} Each algorithm executes continuously for at least 10\,s (GPU) or 2\,s (CPU), after 50 GPU warmup iterations; energy per call is $E = \Delta P \times t / n_{\text{calls}}$.

\subsection{Instruction Counts: Nsight Compute}
\label{sec:setup_ncu}

To check the analytical counts against what the hardware executes, we profile all 37 algorithms with NVIDIA Nsight Compute~\cite{NsightCompute} at $B = 1$ on the RTX 4090, summing FP32 FMA, add, and multiply instructions over every kernel of one invocation; Python loops are profiled over one full period (their kernel sequence repeats exactly) and scaled by the iteration count. This check is independent of the fitted coefficients.

\subsection{Command Counts: Nsight Systems}
\label{sec:census}

$S_o$ is measured with NVIDIA Nsight Systems~\cite{NsightSystems}: for each of the 264 benchmark configurations we set up the algorithm exactly as the harness does, warm up, and trace one invocation, counting kernel launches, memory copies, and memsets. Counts are deterministic across repeats and independent of $N$ for the fixed-iteration Python loops; cuSOLVER switches its SVD algorithm at $N = 1024$ (Householder path, 245 kernels, to batched Jacobi, 137). Counts were taken on the RTX 4090 (PyTorch 2.6, CUDA 12.4) and applied to both GPUs' configurations. Code, data, and traces: \url{https://github.com/jemsbhai/TOMLSignals}.

\subsection{Model Accuracy}

Table~\ref{tab:coefficients} reports the fitted coefficients and Fig.~\ref{fig:scatter} the predictions. Because the measured energies span five decades, we report the error distribution rather than $r^2$ alone: the median absolute error is \mdapea\% on the RTX 4090 and \mdapeb\% on the A100, \withinTwoa\% and \withinTwob\% of configurations fall within a factor of two of measurement, and \withinThreea\% and \withinThreeb\% within a factor of three (linear-space $r^2$ is \rTwoLina\ and \rTwoLinb; $\log_{10}$-space $r^2$ is \rTwoLoga\ and \rTwoLogb). To separate fit from prediction we refit the model 37 times leaving out one algorithm at a time and predict every configuration of the held-out algorithm: the median error rises to \mdapeLOAOa\% and \mdapeLOAOb\%, \withinTwoLOAOa\% and \withinTwoLOAOb\% stay within 2$\times$, and every coefficient stays within its bracket in Table~\ref{tab:coefficients}. Leaving out single configurations instead moves these numbers by under two points: four coefficients do not memorize 138 points. $\alpha_f$ is identified by the LSTM alone, so its fold is the one case the model cannot predict (error about 90\%).

By regime, the Python-loop algorithms are the best predicted (median error \mdapeLoopa\% and \mdapeLoopb\%; \withinTwoLoopa\% and \withinTwoLoopb\% within 2$\times$) because their energy is almost entirely command cost, and the fused LSTM is predicted within \mdapeFuseda\%; the parallel regime carries the residual (\mdapePara\% and \mdapeParb\%), whose origin Section~\ref{sec:discussion} makes precise. A single-coefficient model $E = \alpha \cdot \text{TO}_{\text{total}}$, the calibrated-FLOP-counting analogue, reaches $r^2 = \baseRtwoa$ and \baseRtwob\ with median errors of \baseMdapea\% and \baseMdapeb\%.

The coefficients are physically interpretable. $\alpha_c$ agrees across GPUs within 12\% (\alphaCa\ vs.\ \alphaCb\,fJ/TO), as expected for comparable FP32 units. $\alpha_m$ is 2.6$\times$ larger on the A100, consistent with its wider memory interface and uncounted memory-controller overhead. $\alpha_o$ differs by \alphaOhostRatio$\times$ (\alphaOa\ vs.\ \alphaOb\,$\mu$J per command): a command costs what the GPU idles while the host issues the next one, i.e.\ it is set by the host, and the ratio matches the 7$\times$ per-step ratio measured directly on the Python loops. $\alpha_f$ is a GPU-side serial cost and differs by 1.2$\times$. Accordingly, $\alpha_c$ and $\alpha_m$ transfer between the two systems (A100 coefficients applied to the RTX 4090 with only $\alpha_o$ and $\alpha_f$ refit predict as well as the RTX 4090's own fit: \xferBtoAKeepCMMdape\% median error, \xferBtoAKeepCMWithinTwo\% within 2$\times$, \xferBtoAKeepCMHH\ head-to-head), whereas $\alpha_o$ must be measured on the target host.

\caption{Head-to-head ranking on the RTX 4090. Green: the model identifies the cheaper algorithm of the pair; red: ranking failure.}
\label{fig:headtohead}
\end{figure}

\subsection{Head-to-Head Ranking}

To test whether the model identifies the more energy-efficient algorithm in practical choices, we evaluate 30 head-to-head pairs per GPU (FFT vs.\ direct DFT, FIR direct vs.\ FFT-based, LMS vs.\ RLS, Kalman vs.\ UKF, periodogram vs.\ Welch, CNN vs.\ LSTM, LSTM vs.\ Transformer, Wiener vs.\ CNN, at every common $N$) against the measured ordering. The model ranks \hha\ pairs correctly on the RTX 4090 (Fig.~\ref{fig:headtohead}) and \hhb\ on the A100, \hhPooled\ overall (\hhPooledPct\%); under leave-one-algorithm-out, where each algorithm of a pair is predicted by a model that never saw it, \hhPooledLOAO\ (\hhPooledLOAOPct\%). Seven of the eleven failures are near ties in which the two measured energies differ by less than 10\% (all three on the RTX 4090; Kalman vs.\ UKF at three sizes and LMS vs.\ RLS at $N = 4096$ on the A100) and the model's 4 to 11\% margin has the wrong sign; two more differ by 16 to 25\% (LMS vs.\ RLS at $N = 256$ and 1024 on the A100). The two clear misses are periodogram vs.\ Welch at $N = 256$ on the A100, where the model predicts equal energy for two estimators that share the FFT count and differ only in the averaging (measured 2.2$\times$ apart), and Wiener vs.\ CNN at $N = 16384$ on the A100 (Wiener 1.42$\times$ the CNN, predicted 0.78$\times$), which sits on the residual discussed in Section~\ref{sec:discussion}.

\caption{Analytical FP32 operation counts vs.\ Nsight Compute FP32 instruction counts for all 37 algorithms ($B = 1$). Circles: kernels that are the algorithm; squares: library kernels on small tensors that execute fixed padded tiles; triangles: iterative factorizations. Dashed line: identity.}

\subsection{Instruction-Count Validation}
\label{sec:ncu}

Figure~\ref{fig:ncu} compares the analytical counts with executed FP32 instructions for all 37 algorithms. They fall into three populations.

\textbf{Kernels that are the algorithm} (\ncuAnalyticalN\ algorithms: transforms, convolutions, matrix products, ESPRIT, RLS, DWT, fused IIR, the three denoisers): the median ratio of executed to analytical count is \ncuAnalyticalMedian, with a range of \ncuAnalyticalMin\ (Transformer, whose attention count is conservative) to \ncuAnalyticalMax\ (DST, whose odd-length FFT falls back to a mixed-radix plan~\cite{Duhamel1990}). Two corrections to standard operation counting are confirmed here. \emph{Split-radix FFT:} across a size sweep at $N = 256$, 1024 and 4096, cuFFT's instruction count is \fftRatioTwoFiveSix, \fftRatioOneK\ and \fftRatioFourK\ times the split-radix count $4N \log_2 N - 6N + 8$ (172{,}040 predicted vs.\ 173{,}055 measured at $N = 4096$), against 0.62 to 0.72 times Cooley-Tukey $5N \log_2 N$; at $N \geq 16384$ cuFFT changes plan (a 32-element-per-thread symmetric kernel, then a two-pass $128 \times 256$ factorization) and executes \fftRatioSixteenK\ times the split-radix count, so the analytical count is a bound the library beats. \emph{Complex MAC on FMA hardware:} the textbook 8 real operations per complex MAC overpredict by 2$\times$; with 4~FMAs the direct DFT at $N = 1024$ gives 4{,}194{,}304 predicted vs.\ 4{,}229{,}120 measured (99.2\%).

\textbf{Small-tensor library kernels} (\ncuPaddedN\ algorithms): the Python-loop algorithms, the JPEG codec, and single-channel direct FIR call cuBLAS, cuSOLVER, or cuDNN routines on 4$\times$4 matrices, 32-vectors, or one output channel, and those kernels execute fixed tiles (256-thread GEMM tiles, 32-wide LU panels, 32-output-channel convolution tiles) whatever the problem size: \ncuPaddedMin\ (LMS) to \ncuPaddedMax$\times$ (Kalman) the arithmetic count. This is a fixed cost per command, which is what $\alpha_o$ prices; on the RTX 4090 the Kalman filter's 16.4\,M executed instructions cost about 1\,mJ against 1.6\,J of command cost.

\textbf{Iterative factorizations} (SVD, PCA, MUSIC): cuSOLVER's factorization and eigensolver paths have convergence-dependent cost that no fixed formula captures~\cite{GolubVanLoan2013}; the model uses Householder lower bounds ($6ND^2$ for SVD) and executed counts are \ncuFactMin\ to \ncuFactMax$\times$ higher. The median filter executes no FP32 instructions at all (comparison sorting) and is excluded from the ratio.

\subsection{Signal Length Scaling and FIR Crossover}

Figure~\ref{fig:scaling} shows predicted and measured energy against $N$: the model tracks the $O(N \log N)$ scaling of FFT, the $O(N)$ scaling of FIR, the command-dominated flat scaling of the Kalman filter, and the growth of the CNN and Transformer denoisers over two orders of magnitude in $N$. Figure~\ref{fig:fir} shows the classic FIR selection problem, direct convolution ($O(NM)$ MACs for filter length $M$) against FFT-based overlap-add ($O(N \log N)$): model and measurement both place the crossover between $N = 4096$ and $16384$, because the model carries cuFFT's split-radix cost and the FFT approach's memory traffic.

\label{fig:fir}

\subsection{Three Sequential Energy Regimes}
\label{sec:regimes}

Sequential algorithms on GPUs fall into three regimes. \emph{Parallel:} all work executes in a bounded set of commands per invocation (1 to 14 for batched transforms and filters, up to 245 for cuSOLVER factorizations); for the batched algorithms the command term is a median \launchSharePara\% of the prediction on the RTX 4090, while for the factorizations at $B = 1$ it is most of it. \emph{Python-loop dispatch:} each iteration issues 7 to 54 commands, and command cost dominates energy: \alphaOa\,$\mu$J per command on the RTX 4090 and \alphaOb\,$\mu$J on the A100. \emph{Fused-sequential:} a single kernel processes all $N$ timesteps serially at \alphaFa\ and \alphaFb\,$\mu$J per step. The ratio $\alpha_o / \alpha_f$ is \alphaOoverFa\ on the laptop and \alphaOoverFb\ on the server: a fused step costs a quarter of a command on the former and one and a half commands on the latter. Fusing a Python loop that issues $K$ commands per timestep into one kernel therefore reduces the per-timestep cost by $K \alpha_o / \alpha_f$: for the measured $K$ of 7 (LMS) to 54 (UKF), \fusionGainMina\ to \fusionGainMaxa$\times$ on the laptop host and \fusionGainMinb\ to \fusionGainMaxb$\times$ on the server host. The two mechanisms are distinct in kind (host-side idling versus GPU-side serial execution), and the payoff of fusion is a property of the system, not of the algorithm.

% =========================================================================
\section{CPU vs GPU Analysis}
\label{sec:cpugpu}
% =========================================================================

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig7_cpu_vs_gpu}
\caption{CPU-to-GPU energy ratio by category. Ratios above 1 indicate the GPU is more efficient. Sequential algorithms (adaptive, estimation) are 10 to 100$\times$ more efficient on CPU.}
\label{fig:cpugpu}
\end{figure}

We compare energy per signal between the i9-14900HX CPU ($B = 1$) and the RTX 4090 GPU (energy per call divided by batch size) across 129 common (algorithm, $N$) configurations; Fig.~\ref{fig:cpugpu} shows the ratio by category. Three regimes emerge.

\textbf{Parallel-batched algorithms} (transforms, filters, spectral, ML, compression): the GPU wins 84 of 85 comparisons with a median advantage of 22$\times$; batch parallelism amortizes command overhead across $B$ signals and the GPU's throughput dominates.

\textbf{Sequential algorithms} (adaptive filters, state estimation): the CPU wins all 32 comparisons; the GPU's command cost (\alphaOa\,$\mu$J on this host) dominates. NLMS is 100$\times$ more energy-efficient on CPU, where the per-step overhead is a function call rather than a cross-device command.

\textbf{Decomposition} (SVD, PCA, FastICA, NMF): mixed, with the CPU winning 6 of 8 comparisons; these factorizations do not parallelize across the batch. SVD shows a crossover: the CPU wins at $N = 256$ (ratio 0.59$\times$) and the GPU at $N \geq 1024$ (2.45$\times$) as cuSOLVER amortizes its fixed overhead.

The GPU's advantage decreases with signal length: the median CPU-to-GPU ratio drops from 23$\times$ at $N = 256$ to 4.3$\times$ at $N = 16384$, as per-signal compute grows while batch amortization stays constant.

% =========================================================================
\section{Discussion}
\label{sec:discussion}
% =========================================================================

\textbf{What the residual is.} Figure~\ref{fig:effto} plots measured energy per compute TO for every parallel-regime configuration. Across floating-point kernels the per-algorithm median spans \effDfta\ fJ/TO (direct DFT, a dense complex GEMM at peak throughput) through \effFfta\ (FFT) to about 250 (wavelets), a 60$\times$ range that falls with the work per invocation; sort-based, factorization and serial kernels sit three to five decades higher (SVD \effSvda, PCA \effPcaa, median filter \effMediana\ fJ/TO on the RTX 4090). The fitted $\alpha_c$ (\alphaCa\ fJ/TO) is the energy per operation of the largest, highest-throughput kernels. Energy per counted operation on a GPU is a throughput variable, not a constant; this bounds any constant-cost-per-operation model, TO- or FLOP-based, and is why absolute error reaches a factor of two on a quarter of the configurations while ranking is right \hhPooledPct\% of the time. The DRAM traffic of the composite FFT-based algorithms is 5 to 9$\times$ the analytical $T_m$ (eager execution materializes every intermediate); counting those intermediates is the next refinement of the memory term.

\begin{figure}[!t]
\centering
\includegraphics[width=\columnwidth]{figures/fig9_energy_per_to}
\caption{Measured energy per compute TO against compute TOs per invocation for the parallel regime, both GPUs. Dashed line: fitted $\alpha_c$.}
\label{fig:effto}
\end{figure}

\textbf{Comparison to FLOP counting.} FLOP-based models overcount FFT operations by 30\%, overcount complex arithmetic by 2$\times$ on FMA hardware, and ignore command dispatch, which dominates the energy of adaptive and estimation algorithms; the single-coefficient model above ($r^2$ = \baseRtwoa\ and \baseRtwob; \baseWithinTwoa\% and \baseWithinTwob\% within 2$\times$) is what calibrated FLOP counting achieves on this data.

\textbf{Scope.} (1)~One $\alpha_o$ per system prices every command alike, so pairs of Python-loop algorithms within 10\% of each other are ranked at the model's margin (Kalman vs.\ UKF, LMS vs.\ RLS). (2)~Iterative factorizations (SVD, PCA, MUSIC) have implementation-dependent counts; the model uses analytical lower bounds. (3)~Command counts were measured on the RTX 4090's software stack and applied to the A100's configurations. (4)~CPU energy at small $N$ carries about 37\% relative noise from idle-power variability.

\textbf{Practical implications.} (1)~Sequential algorithms should run on CPU unless a fused CUDA kernel is available; fusion pays \fusionGainMina\ to \fusionGainMaxa$\times$ per timestep on a laptop host and \fusionGainMinb\ to \fusionGainMaxb$\times$ on a server host, so measure $\alpha_o$ on the deployment host before deciding. (2)~FFT-based algorithms should pad to power-of-two lengths; non-power-of-two sizes incur up to 5$\times$ penalties from cuFFT's mixed-radix fallback. (3)~For algorithm selection (FIR direct vs.\ FFT convolution, classical vs.\ learned denoising), the model's rankings agree with measurement \hhPooledPct\% of the time without hardware access; on the RTX 4090 it reproduces the measured ordering of Wiener, CNN, LSTM and Transformer denoisers at every $N$ except a 3\% near tie between CNN and LSTM at $N = 4096$ (the Wiener filter is 8 to 28$\times$ cheaper than the CNN at $N \leq 1024$ and within 10\% of it at $N \geq 4096$; the Transformer is the most expensive at every $N$).

% =========================================================================
\section{Conclusion}
\label{sec:conclusion}
% =========================================================================

We have presented a four-parameter energy model grounded in transistor-level operation costs whose inputs are measured: analytical operation counts checked against Nsight Compute for all 37 algorithms, and per-invocation GPU command counts from Nsight Systems for every configuration. On two GPU architectures it predicts energy with median errors of \mdapea\% and \mdapeb\%, places \withinTwoa\% and \withinTwob\% of configurations within a factor of two, and ranks \hhPooledPct\% of head-to-head pairs correctly, with leave-one-algorithm-out results within a few points. Instruction counts confirm the split-radix FFT and 4-FMA complex MAC corrections and show that library kernels on tiny matrices execute fixed work per launch, which the dispatch term prices. The per-command cost is set by the host (\alphaOa\ vs.\ \alphaOb\,$\mu$J), which sets the payoff of kernel fusion, and sequential algorithms are 10 to 100$\times$ more energy-efficient on CPU. Measured energy per operation spans 60$\times$ across floating-point kernels; making that throughput dependence part of the model is the next step.
